content: Acne vulgaris is a chronic inflammatory condition of the pilosebaceous unit, which is often associated with significant psychosocial and mental health challenges. It affects over 80% of teenagers. Oral isotretinoin is widely regarded as a highly effective treatment for severe acne, but it is also associated with potential adverse effects. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of oral isotretinoin in the treatment of acne vulgaris. A comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Skin Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, and LILACS, was conducted up to July 2017, with an update in March 2018. Additional searches for adverse effects were performed in MEDLINE and Embase up to September 2013. The review included randomized clinical trials (RCTs) comparing oral isotretinoin with placebo, other systemic or topical therapies, or different isotretinoin formulations, doses, regimens, or treatment durations. A total of 31 RCTs involving 3,836 participants aged 12 to 55 years with mild to severe acne were included. Twice as many male participants were enrolled compared to females. Most studies were conducted in Asia, Europe, and North America, with outcomes assessed over 8 to 32 weeks of therapy (mean duration: 19.7 weeks). Comparisons included oral isotretinoin versus placebo, antibiotics, or other treatments, as well as different isotretinoin doses, regimens, or formulations. Twelve of the included trials were funded by pharmaceutical companies. Most studies had a high risk of bias in at least one domain, including attrition bias, selective reporting bias, and performance bias. When comparing oral isotretinoin to oral antibiotics combined with topical agents, three studies involving 400 participants with moderate to severe acne showed no significant reduction in inflammatory lesion counts with isotretinoin compared to antibiotics (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.06). One serious adverse event, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, was reported in the isotretinoin group (RR 3.00, 95% CI 0.12 to 72.98), but the evidence was of very low quality. Isotretinoin may slightly improve acne severity as assessed by physicians (15% improvement; RR 1.15, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.32; 351 participants; 2 studies), but it was associated with a higher risk of minor adverse effects, such as dry lips, dry skin, cheilitis, nausea, and vomiting (67% increased risk; RR 1.67, 95% CI 1.42 to 1.98; 351 participants; 2 studies). These findings were based on low-quality evidence. Regarding different doses and therapeutic regimens of oral isotretinoin, three RCTs assessed efficacy, but heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis. One study involving 154 participants with severe acne reported reductions in inflammatory lesion counts of 79%, 80%, and 84% after 20 weeks of treatment with 0.05, 0.1, and 0.2 mg/kg/day of isotretinoin, respectively (low-quality evidence). Another trial with 150 participants with severe acne compared 0.1, 0.5, and 1 mg/kg/day isotretinoin for 20 weeks, with 58%, 80%, and 90% of participants achieving a 95% reduction in inflammatory lesion counts, respectively. A 24-week RCT in participants with moderate acne compared continuous low-dose isotretinoin (0.25 to 0.4 mg/kg/day), continuous conventional-dose isotretinoin (0.5 to 0.7 mg/kg/day), and an intermittent regimen (0.5 to 0.7 mg/kg/day for one week per month). Continuous low-dose and conventional-dose regimens resulted in greater reductions in inflammatory lesion counts compared to the intermittent regimen (MD 3.72 lesions, 95% CI 2.13 to 5.31; MD 3.87 lesions, 95% CI 2.31 to 5.43; 40 participants; one study each). These findings were based on low-quality evidence. Fourteen RCTs involving 906 participants with moderate to severe acne reported no serious adverse events when comparing different doses or regimens of isotretinoin during treatment (12 to 32 weeks) or follow-up (up to 48 weeks). Thirteen RCTs involving 858 participants assessed the frequency of minor adverse effects, such as skin dryness, hair loss, and itching, but heterogeneity in outcome assessment precluded data pooling, resulting in uncertainty about the findings (lowto very low-quality evidence). Improvement in acne severity, as assessed by physicians, was not measured in these comparisons. None of the included RCTs reported birth defects, but isotretinoin is contraindicated during pregnancy due to its known teratogenic effects. The authors concluded that the evidence for most outcomes was of low quality. There was no clear evidence that isotretinoin improves acne severity compared to standard oral antibiotic and topical treatments when assessed by reductions in inflammatory lesion counts, although it may slightly improve physician-assessed acne severity. Only one serious adverse event was reported in the isotretinoin group, but the risk of serious adverse effects remains uncertain. Isotretinoin was associated with an increased risk of minor adverse effects. Heterogeneity in studies comparing different regimens, doses, or formulations of isotretinoin precluded meta-analysis. Daily treatment may be more effective than intermittent treatment. Further research is needed to evaluate different isotretinoin doses and regimens for acne of all severities, with standardized assessments of efficacy, safety, and patient-reported outcomes.
